clue.text: Love endless free entertainment? Indeed

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a treat is something enjoyable paid for by someone else
sure means indeed, certainly

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether love is endless free fun, and gets a firm yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts the last letter from TREAT to leave TREA. 'Love' is the definition, the affectionate way of addressing someone dear.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone 'treasure' or 'love' are both fond terms of address for a cherished person.

clue.text: Given time, smash great goal

indicators.note: Given means granted at the outset, so the time letter is set in front of what follows
smash means break apart, so the letters are reassembled in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: With enough time, a striker smashes home a great goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smash' looks like a description of the shot, but it tells you to rearrange GREAT after T.
explanation.definitionFit: A target is an aim or objective, something one sets out to achieve.

clue.text: Young bird caught by beagle terrified

indicators.note: Anything caught by something is held fast inside it, so the letters wanted sit unbroken within the words that follow.

parts.note: run the two words together and the six letters you need are consecutive, starting one letter in

explanation.surface: A terrified beagle has caught a chick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrified' looks like it should be shaking the letters up; it is simply the second half of the hiding place. The bird is a specific one, the chick of an eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: An eaglet is an eagle's chick, so 'young bird' names it by its general kind rather than its species.

clue.text: Working on skills, turning up in more than one bed

indicators.note: In a down entry, up runs back towards the top of the grid, so the pieces just built are read the other way.

parts.note: somebody working on a job is at it — a loose equivalence the setter leans on
an art is a practised skill, so the plural answers the plural

explanation.surface: Somebody practising their craft keeps appearing in more than one bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Beds here are geological, the layers a cliff face shows you, not anything in a bedroom or a garden. 'Working on' is the loose piece: to be at something is to be working on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Strata are the layers rock settles in, and geologists call each layer a bed, so a plural definition meets a plural answer.

clue.text: Senior Soviet officer, one previously safely cocooned

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a high-ranking naval commander in the Red (Soviet) navy
second meaning: a butterfly, which spent its pupal stage wrapped in a chrysalis

explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads as Cold War history; the second is the butterfly's life cycle, since it grew inside a chrysalis before emerging.
explanation.definitionFit: The red admiral is a common butterfly, and a Soviet admiral could be called a Red one.

clue.text: Is not sea, but is in it

definitions.text: Is not sea, but is in it

parts.note: the clue's opening word taken as two letters, exactly as written
dry ground, defined here by what it is not — the two of them cover the whole surface of the planet

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and its first three words are also the wordplay, which is what &lit means: read one sentence twice, once for sense and once as instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: An island is land entirely surrounded by water, which is precisely something that is not sea and yet sits in it.

clue.text: No ordinary king's breakfast?

parts.note: whatever is not ordinary is special
K is the standing abbreviation for king, as on a chess scoresheet

explanation.surface: A king sits down to a breakfast rather grander than anyone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting this is one brand of cereal standing in for a whole meal. The apostrophe-s is joinery rather than a possessive to solve.
explanation.definitionFit: Special K is a breakfast cereal, so 'breakfast' names it by the meal it belongs to — one brand for a whole class.

clue.text: Is the crossword setter to appear on television as friendly?

parts.note: the verb changes person: 'is' becomes 'am' once the speaker is the subject
the setter writing the clue speaks of himself in the first person
cable is how television reaches many homes, so appearing on one is appearing on the other

explanation.surface: The person who wrote this puzzle wonders whether he would come across as friendly on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The crossword setter' means I or ME in a Guardian clue, a convention worth owning since it comes round most weeks. Cable is television named by the route it arrives on.
explanation.definitionFit: Amicable describes dealings conducted in a friendly spirit, so the adjective is a plain synonym in its everyday sense.

clue.text: Maid accustomed to home

definitions.meaning: the noun sense: the servant employed to keep a household running
the adjective sense, used of a creature that has settled to living indoors alongside people

explanation.surface: A servant who has grown thoroughly used to the house she works in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maid' hands you the noun and 'accustomed to home' the adjective, with nothing but a space between them. No letters are shuffled, hidden or spelled out anywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A domestic is a household servant, and as an adjective the word covers anything settled about the house, animals included.

clue.text: It's the fashion to purchase from this business

parts.note: clothes are rags in the slang of the people who sell them — glad rags — and the fashion is what you wear
to buy and sell is to trade, so purchasing is half of what the word covers

explanation.surface: Everybody is buying from this shop because that is the fashionable thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's the fashion' reads as a passing craze and means clothing here — the industry has always called what it sells rags, cheerfully enough to put the word in its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: The rag trade is the British name for the clothing business, so 'this business' points at the industry the clue has been describing.

clue.text: Person entranced that is often called happy

definitions.meaning: the spiritualist who goes into a trance to carry messages from the dead
the middle course between two extremes, which English pairs with 'happy' so often that the adjective points straight at the noun

explanation.surface: Somebody deep in a trance is described as blissfully content.
explanation.walkthrough: The séance and the middle way are the two senses, and the idiom 'a happy medium' is what the second half is pointing at — the phrase does the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A medium is the person who goes into a trance to reach the dead, and also the middle course between extremes that idiom calls happy.

clue.text: Flow that's regular late in the day

parts.note: a regular pulse is an even one, steady and unvarying
the sea's twice-daily flow is the tide

explanation.surface: A steady current keeps running as the day gets late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flow' is clued first and lands second in the answer, so the build runs against the reading. The word itself is poetic — hymns and Victorian verse rather than weather forecasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventide is an old word for evening, so the definition names the stretch of time it covers rather than an event.

clue.text: Late stages of World Cup seen in Netherlands, Belarus and Wales

parts.note: not which name the letter is in but where in each name it is seen — the position, spelled out as a word
the one letter all three of these names close with

explanation.surface: Three countries are named as places where the closing rounds of the World Cup were watched.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words and the clue explains itself: the letter S is what is final in Netherlands, Belarus and Wales. The World Cup half is a straight definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The finals are the closing knockout rounds of a tournament, which is exactly the late stages of a World Cup.

clue.text: A cold salad plant not quite consumed: hurry up!

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

indicators.note: not quite means the word stops short of its final letter

parts.note: celery is a salad vegetable
ate means consumed

explanation.surface: Someone barely finishes a chilled celery salad before being told to get a move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims CELERY to CELER, and the exclamation is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Accelerate means speed up or go faster, which is what someone told to hurry must do.

clue.text: Relish saying 'Choose a flower'

indicators.note: Something said is heard rather than read, so the quoted words count for their sound and not for their spelling.

parts.note: to choose is to pick, and the flower is the lily; said at speed the three words run into one

explanation.surface: A speaker takes pleasure in telling someone to go and pick a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the quoted words at speed and they turn into the name of a mustard-yellow pickle. 'Relish' is both the definition and, in its other sense, what the speaker is doing.
explanation.definitionFit: Piccalilli is a pickled vegetable relish, so 'relish' names it by the class of condiment it belongs to.

clue.text: Cost to hold part of play rehearsal

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to have it inside you, so one piece here is wrapped around another rather than laid beside it.

parts.note: the cost of a thing is its price, and this word is about to be opened up
a play comes divided into acts, so a part of one is an act

explanation.surface: The ticket price covers a single act of the play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of play' looks like an instruction to take some letters out of the word 'play'; it is an act, the division a drama comes in. 'Cost' is a noun, the price on the ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: A practice is the session where a team or a cast runs through it all before the real thing — a rehearsal.

clue.text: Showing a natural ability to draw?

definitions.meaning: the surface offers innate talent, the child who could always sketch; 'natural' also means belonging to nature, and this is one of its forces
not drawing on paper: to draw is to pull towards you, which is what iron filings feel

explanation.surface: Someone is praised as a born artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' moves from pencils to attraction and 'natural' from talent to physics: the pull a lodestone exerts on iron is entirely a property of nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Something magnetic draws things to itself — iron to a magnet, people to a person — and does so by its nature.

clue.text: Avoid son, despite staggering

indicators.note: Somebody staggering cannot hold a straight line, and the letters beside the word do not hold their order either.

parts.note: S is the standing abbreviation for son, as on a family tree
the seven letters of the preposition, thrown in with the S as fodder

explanation.surface: Even while lurching about, somebody manages to keep out of their son's way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Despite' reads as a conjunction arguing with the first half of the sentence, and it is the fodder; the extra letter it needs is the son standing next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidestep something is to avoid it by moving aside and letting it pass, rather than by refusing it.

clue.text: With new energy, admire neat dancing

indicators.note: Dancers keep swapping places, and the letters in front of the word take new positions in the same way.

parts.note: ten letters exactly, which is the enumeration, waiting to be reordered

explanation.surface: Watching some tidy dancing with fresh enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With new energy' looks like a lead-in — 'new' is a favourite anagram signal — and is in fact the definition, with the shuffle instruction saved for the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something reanimated has been brought back to life, so it carries on with new energy where it had stopped.

clue.text: Pageant shows tasteless stuff as well

parts.note: tat is British for cheap and nasty goods, the junk at the back of a market stall
both mean in addition

explanation.surface: A pageant turns out to be full of cheap junk as well.
explanation.walkthrough: A tattoo here is the military display of massed pipes and marching bands, the Edinburgh sort, rather than the ink on somebody's arm that 'tasteless' nudges you towards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo is a military pageant of drill, bands and drums put on for an audience, so 'pageant' names its kind.

clue.text: Walk a little, holding lime or soda perhaps

indicators.note: Whatever is held sits inside its holder, so the letters wanted run unbroken through the words just before.

parts.note: run the three words together and six consecutive letters spell what you need, starting one letter into the first

explanation.surface: Somebody strolls a short way holding a lime or a soda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lime or soda perhaps' is a definition by example — both are bases in the chemical sense, which is what the 'perhaps' is apologising for. The drink belongs to the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: Lime and soda are both alkalis, so the clue defines the class by naming two members, with 'perhaps' flagging the leap.

clue.text: Will's play full of errors? Dante's was divine

definitions.meaning: Will is Shakespeare, and one of his titles is completed by the word wanted plus 'of Errors'
the Florentine poet's great work is his, and it is described by the adjective sitting here

explanation.surface: Shakespeare wrote a play full of mistakes, while Dante's was heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's is The Comedy of Errors and Dante's is The Divine Comedy, so each half of the clue hands you a famous title with the same word lifted out.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors and Dante's Divine Comedy both complete their titles with the word, which names a work with a happy ending.

clue.text: Reportedly overcome hard nut

indicators.note: A word reported is one you hear said, so what is wanted is the sound and not the spelling.

parts.note: to overcome an enemy is to conquer them, and in British speech that word and the six letters wanted are one sound

explanation.surface: A tough character is said to have been beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: British children play conkers by threading horse chestnuts on string and swinging them at each other's, so the hard nut is a literal one. Say 'conquer' aloud and you have the spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A conker is the hard shiny seed of the horse chestnut, so 'hard nut' describes it exactly.

clue.text: Gaoler is to reorganise women's quarters

indicators.note: Reorganising a thing keeps every part of it and changes only the arrangement, which is what the letters before it undergo.

parts.note: eight letters, matching the enumeration, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A prison officer is told to sort out the women's wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaoler' is the British spelling of jailer, which is where the O and the A come from. A seraglio is the sealed women's part of an Ottoman palace, the harem.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraglio is the shut-off part of a Turkish palace where the women lived, which is a set of women's quarters.

clue.text: Completely at home with Dorothy's pet

parts.note: somebody at home is in, the standing crossword sense of the word
the little dog Dorothy carries through the Land of Oz

explanation.surface: Somebody is entirely comfortable in the company of Dorothy's dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin tag means 'in total' and survives in legal English — a claim rejected in toto. 'Completely at home' reads as one phrase, which is where the split hides.
explanation.definitionFit: In toto is Latin for 'in total', used in English to mean wholly or entirely — 'completely' with a gown on.

clue.text: Ancient city prison: pictures initially hung in it?

indicators.note: in it means placed inside the thing just named, so these letters go into the prison word

parts.note: a cage is a prison or place of confinement
art means pictures, as in an art gallery

indicators.note: initially means take only the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the first letter of hung

explanation.surface: A jail in the ancient world with paintings hanging on its walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' refers back to the prison, so 'in it' puts the pictures and the first letter of 'hung' inside. Carthage was the Phoenician city in North Africa that Rome destroyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Carthage, near modern Tunis, was a great city of antiquity and Rome's chief rival.

clue.text: Key exercise, to trap a fly

indicators.note: Trapping a thing shuts it in, so the letter it points at is enclosed by the pieces on either side.

parts.note: the key at the top left of a keyboard, the one that gets you out of a dialogue box
PE is the standing abbreviation for exercise, physical education at school
the clue's own indefinite article, caught between the two other pieces

explanation.surface: An important drill designed to catch a fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' is the button on a keyboard rather than a door key or a musical one, and 'fly' is the verb: birds do it, and so do prisoners.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly is to make off in a hurry — the suspect flew — which is what escaping is, verb for verb.

clue.text: Love to break down large town fastness?

indicators.note: to break down means the word falls apart, so its letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written
a city is a large town

explanation.surface: Romance falling apart in a big town, and a stronghold under threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to break down' rearranges LOVE into VELO. 'fastness' usually means a fortress, but the question mark points to the sense of being fast, speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Velocity is speed of movement, so being fast taken as a quantity.
